### Q1
```{r}
library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")
```

```{r}
# Data Overview
glimpse(ny_noaa)

# Check Missing Data
ny_noaa |>
  summarize(
    id_missing = sum(is.na(id)),
    date_missing = sum(is.na(date)),
    prcp_missing = sum(is.na(prcp)),
    snow_missing = sum(is.na(snow)),
    snwd_missing = sum(is.na(snwd)),
    tmax_missing = sum(is.na(tmax)),
    tmin_missing = sum(is.na(tmin))
  )
```
The ny_noaa dataset contains daily weather observations recorded at weather stations across New York State, with 2,595,176 observations and 7 variables: station ID, observation date, precipitation, snowfall, snow depth, maximum temperature, and minimum temperature. Only station ID and observation date have no missing values, while all other variables contain substantial missing data. In particular, nearly half of the observations are missing temperature measurements. Since we do not know why these values are missing or whether there are any underlying patterns in the missingness, the missing temperature data may introduce bias into our overall assessment of climate conditions, potentially leading to overestimation or underestimation of temperature extremes.
```{r}
# Data Cleaning
ny_noaa = ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10
  )
ny_noaa = ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    prcp = prcp / 10
  )
ny_noaa = ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    year = year(date),
    month = month(date),
    day = day(date)
  )

glimpse(ny_noaa)

# Snowfall Common Value
ny_noaa |>
  group_by(snow) |>
  summarize(n = n()) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
```
The most commonly observed snowfall value is 0 mm, which has 2,008,508 observations. This makes sense because the dataset includes observations throughout the year, and New York only expects snowfall in several winter days.
```{r}
# January and July Plots
noaa_temp = ny_noaa |>
  filter(month == 1 | month == 7)

noaa_temp = noaa_temp |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

noaa_temp |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature in January and July",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Maximum Temperature (°C)"
  )
```
The plot shows a clear seasonal difference in average maximum temperatures between January and July. In January, average maximum temperatures fluctuate around 0°C, while in July, they generally range between 25°C and 30°C. This is reasonable given the natural temperature differences between winter and summer. Weather stations show similar year-to-year fluctuations within each month, with no obvious long-term increasing or decreasing trend. A few potential outliers can also be observed, particularly an unusually low temperature in January during the early 1980s and another unusually low temperature in July during the late 1980s.
```{r}
# Temperature Plot
# I first tried scatterplot, but the dataset was too large and R was stuck for nearly an hour. I then realized that it needs to be grouped into bins before plotting.
temp_plot = ny_noaa |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin2d(bins = 40) +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum vs. Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Minimum Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum Temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Count"
  )
print(temp_plot)

# Snow Plot
snow_plot = ny_noaa |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_violin() +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall Distribution by Year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  )
print(snow_plot)

# Two-panel Plot
temp_plot / snow_plot
```
